title: How much model does warning triage need? A cost-aware comparison from rules to locally run language models
abstract: Static analysis tools report far more warnings than developers act on, and machine learning is widely proposed to identify the actionable ones. Published comparisons rarely include a simple label-based reference, and rarely report quality on unseen projects together with compute time. This study compares five levels of model complexity on two open datasets, NASCAR (Java) and AW4C (C): a warning-type prior, a linear model on term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) features, a frozen code encoder, fine-tuned code encoders, and open-weight large language models (LLMs) run locally. All models were scored on the same 1,000 warnings per dataset and protocol, using the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) with project-level bootstrap intervals. Three findings emerged. First, in the original AW4C release the number of lines in the supplied code context predicted the label with an MCC of 0.91 on unseen projects, and fine-tuned CodeBERT reached 0.81; in a variant rebuilt with a uniform context window, which also differs in composition, the corresponding values were 0.12 and 0.30. Second, on unseen NASCAR projects an advantage of fine-tuned encoders over the warning-type prior was not established: the paired difference in MCC was −0.08 (95% CI −0.21 to 0.02) for CodeBERT. Third, locally run LLMs without task-specific training scored near zero on NASCAR with the default threshold and required about 47 times the mean processing time of a fine-tuned encoder. Model complexity should be assessed against a simple reference under cross-project evaluation.
authors: Peter Sullivan; Bogdan Mikhaylov

title: MOS: Towards Effective Smart Contract Vulnerability Detection through Mixture-of-Experts Tuning of Large Language Models
abstract: Smart contract vulnerabilities pose significant security risks to blockchain systems, potentially leading to severe financial losses. Existing methods face several limitations: (1) Program analysis-based approaches heavily rely on predefined patterns, lacking flexibility and adaptability to new vulnerability types; (2) Deep learning-based methods lack explanations for their detection results; (3) Large language model-based approaches suffer from high false positive rates. To address these challenges, we propose MOS, a smart contract vulnerability detection framework based on mixture-of-experts tuning (MOE-Tuning) of large language models. First, we conduct Continual Pre-training on a large-scale smart contract dataset to provide a domain-enhanced initialization for the subsequent MOE-Tuning process. Second, to provide reliable explanations for detected vulnerabilities, we construct a high-quality MOE-Tuning dataset through a multi-stage pipeline combining large language model generation and expert verification. Third, we design a vulnerability-aware routing mechanism that activates the most relevant expert networks by analyzing code features and their matching degree with experts, addressing the limitation of predefined patterns in program analysis approaches. Finally, we extend the feed-forward layers of the LLM after Continual Pre-training into multiple parallel expert networks, each specializing in specific vulnerability patterns. We also employ a dual-objective loss function: one for optimizing vulnerability detection and explanation performance, and another for balancing expert utilization through an auxiliary loss based on the scaled dot product of expert assignment frequencies and average routing probabilities, thereby improving model performance in complex vulnerability scenarios. Extensive experiments show that MOS consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in four foundational and historically significant vulnerability types (Reentrancy, Timestamp, Integer Overflow/Underflow, Delegatecall) with average improvements of 6.38% in F1 score and 4.84% in accuracy. The vulnerability explanations generated by MOS also demonstrate high quality, achieving positive ratings (scores of 3 and 4 on a 4-point scale) of 82.96%, 85.21% and 94.58% for correctness, completeness, and conciseness, respectively, through a combined approach of human evaluation and LLM evaluation. Extensibility experiments show that MOS effectively handles new vulnerability types (Access Control, Price Oracle Manipulation, Logic Errors, Lack of Input Validation, Slippage, and Risky First Deposit), consistently outperforming all baseline methods across six additional vulnerability categories. MOS achieved an average F1 score of 83.94% and an average accuracy of 87.82%, demonstrating its strong extensibility and flexibility in handling new vulnerabilities.
authors: Hang Yuan; Lei Yu; Zhirong Huang; Jingyuan Zhang; Junyi Lu; Shiqiang Cheng; Li Yang; Fengjun Zhang; Jiajia Ma; Chun Zuo
venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology

title: Detecting Insecure Compositions of Clean Agent Skills via Capability-Flow Graph Analysis
abstract: AI agents increasingly extend their capabilities by invoking third-party skills, where each skill encapsulates instructions, scripts, and resources for agents to execute on demand. This paper reveals that deploying many benign skills together introduces compositional security risks: multiple individually clean skills can compose into safety-violation chains, because the agent passes an upstream skill's output to a downstream skill's input across invocations. The risk arises not from any single skill, but from the agent's runtime orchestration, and thus cannot be captured by existing malicious skill detection methods. To this end, we develop KnotScryer to detect insecure skill compositions by treating skills as typed capability flows. In particular, we abstract each skill into a capability summary, and construct the Skill Capability-Flow Graph (SCFG), where edges denote cross-skill information flow. Moreover, we design a search policy that tracks protected or untrusted data along handoff edges to locate paths reaching insecure operations. Finally, a two-layer verification method replays the insecure information flow for reachability analysis and applies a task-anchored LLM chain audit to confirm the semantic plausibility of the identified violation chains. We deploy KnotScryer to analyze 13,598 clean skills from ClawHub, and validate the detected chains across three agent frameworks and three LLMs. KnotScryer identifies 612 insecure compositions, which are consistently exploited across agent frameworks. Meanwhile, under GLM-5.1, it outperforms tag-match and graph-only baselines by improving the exploitation rate from 16.5%-18.2% to 85.6%, while reducing the search space by 85.3%. Furthermore, 13.7% of the detected chains consist entirely of skills labeled safe by a single-skill scanner, showing that KnotScryer effectively identifies insecure compositions that per-skill auditing cannot.
authors: Yihao Li; Chuanpu Fu; Yizhou Zhao; Miao Chen; Qi Li; Ke Xu

title: Implementation of an Effective Code Vulnerability Detection Model Using Deep Learning and Attention Mechanism
abstract: With increasing computational power, deep learning methods have been widely applied to software vulnerability detection. Compared to traditional machine learning, deep learning offers low computational overhead, high accuracy, and eliminates the need for manual feature engineering. However, many existing approaches lack sufficient utilization of code syntax and semantics, limiting performance. This study proposes VDDA (Vulnerability Detection based on Deep learning and Attention mechanisms), an effective model that combines deep learning with attention mechanisms. VDDA employs a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BLSTM) network to capture code features automatically. Source code is transformed into Code Property Graphs (CPG) using the Joern tool to retain rich syntactic and semantic information. To enhance feature representation, several strategies are applied: depth-first traversal-based CPG optimization, three-directional code slicing, code block-based slice organization, and separation of function and variable names during symbolization. These methods convert source code into vector representations suitable as input to the deep model. An attention mechanism is integrated with BLSTM to emphasize the most relevant parts of the input vectors for improved vulnerability detection. Experiments on two datasets of varying sizes demonstrate that VDDA achieves superior detection performance compared to existing methods, validating its effectiveness and generalizability in software vulnerability detection tasks.
authors: Erzhou Zhu; Le-Hao Qi; Jia-Qi Chang; Zhu-juan Ma

title: The Dual-Use Nature of Large Language Models in Cybersecurity: A Bibliometric Analysis and Critical Review
abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) now occupy three positions in cybersecurity at once: they are systems that must be secured, capabilities that lower the cost of offence, and instruments that augment defence. Existing reviews typically examine one of these roles in isolation, which obscures how the roles interact and leaves the field without an evidence base for judging whether the interactions are being studied. This article addresses that gap by combining a VOSviewer-based bibliometric analysis with a critical literature review. We retrieved 13,756 records published between January 2023 and 19 October 2026 from OpenAlex and, after document-type, language, abstract, de-duplication and validated relevance screening (precision 84.0%, 95% CI 78.3–88.4%), analysed 7,369 documents through performance analysis, keyword co-occurrence and co-citation mapping in VOSviewer and a dictionary-based classification of each document's dual-use role. The co-occurrence map resolves into four thematic clusters: attacks on and alignment of LLMs; LLM-enabled detection and security operations; code and vulnerability analysis, including penetration testing; and socio-technical threats and governance. Research on LLMs as targets (42.8% of documents) and as defensive tools (35.3%) has grown largely in parallel: only 7.9% of documents address more than one role, and only 11.1% of defensive studies engage with attacks on the defending model itself, falling to 2.5% for vulnerability detection. The critical review explains why this matters: reported success rates of offensive LLM agents range from 0% to 90% depending on experimental design, few defences are evaluated against adaptive adversaries, and the security–utility trade-off is rarely quantified. We formalise these findings in a coupled dual-use framework with three testable propositions and derive eight research directions, prioritising adaptive evaluation, multilingual guardrail robustness, longitudinal measurement and the security of defensive LLM deployments.
authors: Muhammad Sharjeel Aziz; Muhammad Ali; Adnan R. Manzoor; Muhammad Younis; Zulfiya Khabirova

title: A Layered Security Framework and Metrics for Analysing Cross-site Scripting Attacks
abstract: Single Page Applications (SPAs) have become a dominant architecture for modern client-side web systems by shifting state management, routing, and user interface processing to the browser. Although frameworks such as Angular provide built-in security mechanisms, including contextual escaping, template sanitization, and secure data binding, developers may introduce security weaknesses through practices such as unsafe DOM manipulation, dynamic script loading, and improper use of bypass mechanisms. Existing approaches to SPA security assessment primarily focus on identifying known vulnerability patterns through static analysis, providing limited insight into architectural security weaknesses and accumulated security complexity. This study contributes a Metrics-Driven Layered Security Framework (LSF) for assessing and improving the security architecture of Angular SPAs against Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attacks. The proposed framework organizes SPA security controls into three architectural layers: the Rendering Layer, Control Logic Layer, and Outer Shell Layer. It introduces seven security metrics, including Sanitization Bypass Density, Unmanaged Active Sink Frequency, Maximum Nesting Depth, Cyclomatic Branching Factor, CSP Policy Strictness Score, Boundary Validation Density, and Dependency Vulnerability Coefficient, which are combined into composite layer risk scores for comprehensive security assessment. The framework was empirically evaluated through controlled experiments involving Angular developers, comparing developers using the LSF-supported Layered Security Metrics Tool (LSMT) against developers performing unaided manual security reviews. The findings demonstrated that the proposed metrics and framework improve developers’ ability to identify structurally complex XSS-related weaknesses across Angular SPA security layers. The results demonstrate that the LSF provides a measurable approach for proactive vulnerability identification, architectural security auditing, and integration into Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) security processes.
authors: Nevy Kimani Maina; Geoffrey Muchiri Muketha; Jane Wanjiru Njuki

title: DeepAVR: Deep Analysis via Multi-Agent Collaboration for Automated Vulnerability Repair
abstract: Automated Vulnerability Repair (AVR) has emerged as a critical defense against software security flaws, aiming to triage and fix bugs autonomously. Early LLM-based approaches focused on patch generation under the assumption of perfect fault localization, while recent end-to-end methods attempt to repair vulnerabilities directly from sanitizer logs. However, these methods often fail when the root cause is deeply hidden--either physically distant from the crash site or logically masked by interdependent errors--making the initial report insufficient. We propose DeepAVR, a multi-agent framework for end-to-end AVR that performs deep analysis by transforming intermediate repair outcomes into structured diagnostic feedback. DeepAVR decomposes repair into specialized roles--Fault Localization, Patch Generation, Compile Validation, Security Validation, Functionality Validation, and Patch Review--and routes feedback across these roles to iteratively refine both localization and patch hypotheses. In particular, DeepAVR introduces patch-conditioned re-localization, which treats execution results from intermediate patches as diagnostic signals to uncover hidden root causes, and a root-cause-oriented patch review stage that detects symptom-level fixes and incomplete repairs beyond execution-based validation. Evaluation on the real-world C/C++ vulnerability repair dataset VulnLoc shows that DeepAVR significantly outperforms prior methods, generating correct patches for 92.3% of vulnerabilities. Furthermore, results on SAN2VULN demonstrate strong generalization, with DeepAVR effectively repairing vulnerabilities unseen during training.
authors: Woorim Han; Hyunjun Kim; Brian Junekyu Lee; Kyeongmin Kim; Younghan Lee; Hyungon Moon; Yunheung Paek

title: Then there is prompt injection, a malicious email, ...: The Wild Wide West of OpenClaw Agentic System Security
abstract: AI-powered personal assistant frameworks such as OpenClaw combine LLM reasoning, persistent memory, tool invocation, local execution, and web-based workflows. These capabilities enable useful automation, but they also create security risks when untrusted inputs, model reasoning, tools, memory, and deployment configuration interact without explicit trust boundaries. This paper presents an empirical study of reported security concerns in OpenClaw using two complementary data sources: Reddit discussions and security-tagged GitHub issues. We analyze more than 25K Reddit posts from 13 OpenClaw-related subreddits and identify 162 security-relevant posts with 1,787 associated comments. We further collect 358 security-tagged GitHub issues and retain 180 issues describing concrete security concerns. Using qualitative analysis and evidence-grounded CWE mapping, we identify 521 CWE instances across 59 distinct weakness types, concentrated in access-control failures, sensitive-data exposure, injection, and unsafe execution. We also extract 543 practitioner mitigation suggestions and consolidate them into seven recurring strategies. To complement the empirical analysis, we present an evidence-grounded illustrative reconstruction of a representative sensitive-data exposure pathway using dummy secret values. Our findings show that OpenClaw security issues are not isolated implementation bugs; they reflect recurring trust-boundary failures across the agent execution pipeline. We discuss how these weaknesses map to both traditional software-security categories and agent-specific failure mechanisms, and derive implications for safer agentic systems, including explicit trust boundaries, least-privilege tool access, execution containment, runtime oversight, and defense-in-depth deployment.
authors: Mostafijur Rahman Akhond; Mahmuda Khatun; Gias Uddin

title: CIVER: Causal Intervention Verification for Reliable Code Review
abstract: Code review is essential for maintaining software repositories by identifying defects, improving code quality, and supporting reliable software evolution. With the growing adoption of LLM-based coding agents, an increasing number of code contributions and repository changes are generated by these agents. Consequently, LLM-based code review agents are becoming increasingly prevalent to evaluate these contributions and maintain software quality. However, LLM reviewers often generate lengthy reviews containing numerous potential issues, many of which are false positives or lack sufficient evidence. These unreliable reviews can mislead developers and downstream coding agents, motivating the need to distinguish actionable findings from unsupported claims. We propose CIVER, a causal intervention-based framework that identifies the core issues underlying code-review findings and distinguishes genuine defects from false positives. CIVER integrates three modules: a review module assesses findings, an intervention module generates repair-oriented perturbations, and a verifier module scores review reliability. Through joint optimization via expert iteration, the three modules identify genuine defects by responding to targeted repairs while remaining stable under unrelated changes. Extensive experiments on SWE-Review-Bench demonstrate that CIVER correctly identifies 77% of genuine defects through targeted repairs. Cross-project and downstream repair evaluations further demonstrate that CIVER generalizes across repositories and improves coding agents' task success rates, highlighting its effectiveness for reliable automated code review.
authors: Xinyuan Song; Hasibul Haque; Jay Somasundaram; Ryan Turner; Bowen Zhu; Liang Zhao

title: SpeC2Rust: Specification-Driven Repository-Level C-to-Rust Translation
abstract: Legacy C codebases remain central to system software and performance-critical infrastructure, but their weak memory safety imposes security and maintenance risks. Recent C-to-Rust translation systems, including LLM-based translators, make automated migration increasingly feasible, yet they still struggle to recover repository-level intent, avoid raw pointers and unsafe constructs, maintain cross-file interfaces, and repair compilation and validation failures efficiently. We propose SpeC2Rust, a specification-driven pipeline for repository-level C-to-Rust translation. It has three stages: (1) Project-Intent Structuring, which decomposes a C repository into semantically coherent modules and generates persistent repository- and module-level specifications; (2) Spec-Guided Generation, which translates each Rust module against these specifications with a live symbol registry to preserve cross-file consistency; and (3) Layered-Feedback Repair, which batches repairs and injects only failure-relevant diagnostics, specification context, and source evidence for efficient compilation and test-driven correction. We evaluate SpeC2Rust on eight repository-level C projects. It generates Rust projects that compile and pass the original end-to-end tests, with no raw-pointer declarations, raw-pointer dereferences, or unsafe lines. On projects shared with an LLM-based baseline, SpeC2Rust reduces cost by 66.1% and input-token usage by 84.7%.
authors: Junjie Yao; Xiongzheng Guan; Jia Feng; Yujia Chen; Hongliang Tian; Cuiyun Gao

title: Ulysses: A Security Harness For Synthesizing Verifiable Web Exploits
abstract: How can an AI agent automatically discover security vulnerabilities in any software repository? Existing approaches use LLMs to generate software vulnerability exploits. However, it is challenging for an LLM to reliably verify its own generated exploits. In this paper, we propose Ulysses, a multi-agent security harness to synthesize verifiable vulnerability exploits for web applications. Ulysses converts candidate vulnerability findings into verified Proofs of Exploitability by iteratively exploring exploit hypotheses and establishing success in independently observed execution effects. We evaluated Ulysses on WebExploitGym, a curated benchmark of exploitable instances from 25 real-world web applications that span 5 languages and 7 frameworks. Ulysses produces verified proofs for 10 of 25 real-world advisories. It also discovered 4 new proofs of exploitability that have never been previously reported.
authors: Aditya Oke; Andre Vicente Duarte; Rui Melo; Shubham Gandhi; Nachiket Kotalwar; Charmi Khandor; Danqing Wang; Carolyn Rosé; Lei Li

title: An Open-Agent Framework for Intelligent Compliance Analysis in Infrastructure as Code Using Large Language Models
abstract: Abstract Cloud misconfiguration is a leading cause of data breaches in production cloud environments, and Infrastructure as Code (IaC) has amplified this risk by letting a single insecure configuration propagate across an entire cloud estate in one deployment. This paper presents an open-agent framework for intelligent compliance analysis of IaC configurations, integrating Open Policy Agent (OPA)-based Policy-as-Code enforcement with Large Language Model (LLM)-driven contextual reasoning in a single hybrid pipeline. Prior work has treated deterministic policy enforcement and LLM-based analysis independently; the proposed framework instead combines the precision of OPA-based Rego rule evaluation with the explanatory and remediation capabilities of an LLM to produce structured, audit-ready compliance evidence aligned to a formal control framework. The framework is instantiated with a custom 16-rule Rego policy library spanning three NIST SP~800-53 control families Access Control (AC), System and Communications Protection (SC), and Audit and Accountability (AU) across eight AWS resource types, and evaluated on 231 labeled Terraform configurations derived from the IaC-Eval benchmark. The OPA enforcement layer achieves 96.9\% precision, 90.5\% recall, and 93.6\% F1 score. The LLM enrichment layer, guided by a deterministic safeguard against LLM recall errors and explicit prompt-level format constraints, produces reliable, audit-ready control mappings and remediation guidance across 16 violation types. The performance advantage over an industrial static-analysis baseline (Checkov) is confirmed statistically significant via McNemar's exact test ($\chi^2=13.0$, $p<0.001$), demonstrating that the hybrid approach delivers compliance analysis outcomes that neither paradigm achieves alone.
authors: Ayah AlJabali; Muawya N. Al Dalaien

title: Uncovering Why LLMs Fail: From Internal Mechanisms to Adversarial Reasoning Trajectories
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are usually evaluated by final-output correctness or safety, yet an endpoint label does not reveal how a failure develops throughout the reasoning process. We therefore ask whether ordinary reasoning failures and adversarially induced failures can be characterized using the same internal coordinates. Towards this end, we in this paper study a white-box diagnostic framework CauTrace to disclose the root-cause of why LLM fails from three fundamental inspections: Functional States, Propagation of Representation, Temporal-State Coordination and Reasoning Trajectory. First, seven functional states are creatively defined to represent the support and constraint processing in LLMs. Second, the propagation of representation change measures how the changes among the seven states persist across subsequent Transformer blocks. Third, temporal-state coordination and trajectory topology characterize when the commitment and verification occur relative to the support, and how the dominant state sequence evolves over the full inference process. Finally, we evaluate CauTrace on both clean reasoning failures and paired adversarial perturbations. Across Qwen and LLaMA-family models, the failed traces show weaker Attention-MLP agreement on support-state updates and less verification activity relative to commitment, while the exact representation-level signatures and timing shifts vary by architecture. Held-out repair and steering tests demonstrate consistent operational signals that were in line with our claims for certain models and specific settings, with aligned steering producing the predicted directional changes in process measures. Overall, CauTrace provides a unified diagnostic framework for analyzing failure dynamics through changes in support, commitment, and verification, which would shed light on the in-depth research on LLM security.
authors: Zirui Ding; Xinxin Fan; Hao Yuan; Shaoye Luo; Men Niu; Quanliang Jing; Yunfeng Lu

title: Chakraview: A Hybrid Static-Analysis and Local-Llm Prototype for Vulnerability Detection and Mitigation Guidance in Open-Source Software
abstract: Open-source software benefits from rapid, distributed development, but reviewing it for security weaknesses is labour-intensive, and developers need findings that are explained and actionable. We present Chakraview, a prototype that combines a rule-based static stream with a locally hosted large language model (DeepSeek-Coder 6.7B Instruct served through Ollama). Uploaded Python, C/C++, PHP, and Java files or ZIP archives are parsed with Tree-sitter, analysed by both streams, fused by a weighted score (0.6 × LLM confidence + 0.4 × static flag), and reported with CWE labels, explanations, and suggested mitigations. We document the architecture, analyse the fusion rule, and report two preliminary checks: seven functional checks recorded in project documentation, and a reproducible measurement of the static stream on four developer-written files containing 29 seeded vulnerable lines, of which 23 were flagged (22 under the correct CWE); all misses were injection-type flaws needing data-flow reasoning. The LLM stream, the fusion score, and the generated fixes have not been evaluated on labeled data, and suggested fixes are not compiled, tested, or rescanned. Chakraview is therefore a preliminary system prototype, not a validated detector. We specify a held-out evaluation protocol comparing static-only, LLM-only, and fused analysis, with separate tests of localization, calibration, and mitigation correctness.
authors: Ajay Vinod Dawkhare Amit Rushikesh Tayade; Aryan Mandar Wable; Sakshi Sopan Bhor Mayur Shashikant Thakare
venue: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology

title: AI-Powered Penetration Testing and Vulnerability Remediation for GitHub Repositories
abstract: AI-Powered Penetration Testing and Vulnerability Remediation for GitHub Repositories presents PentestAI, a web platform that scans a developer's GitHub repositories for security vulnerabilities, verifies the serious findings in an isolated sandbox and proposes fixes as pull requests.The system combines a Large Language Model (Google Gemini) that analyses the most securityrelevant source files with a deterministic pattern-matching pass that detects committed secrets such as API keys and private keys.High and critical findings are re-checked with CodeQL and Semgrep inside network isolated Docker containers to reduce false positives.A fixer service generates a patch with a code model, re-scans the patched code twice and opens a pull request only if the vulnerability is gone and no new issue is introduced.The application is built with TanStack Start, React and Supabase, and supports weekly automated scans, vulnerability lifecycle tracking, reports and an AI security assistant.The results show that the platform turns a manual, expensive security audit into a fast, repeatable and verifiable process for everyday developers.
authors: Mrs. Bindu K.P; Gagana R; Kushal K R; M G Sahana; M Harshit Pramod

title: Automated creation of source code variants of a cryptographic hash function implementation using generative pre-trained transformer models
abstract: Generative pre-trained transformers (GPTs) are a type of large language machine learning model that are unusually adept at producing novel, and coherent, natural language. However, GPT model outputs in general are stochastic and not always correct. For programming languages, the exact specification of the computer code, syntactically and algorithmically, is strictly required in order to ensure the security of computing systems and applications. Therefore, using GPT models to generate computer code poses an important security risk—while at the same time allowing for potential innovation in how computer code is generated. This study examines GPT model outputs of novel and correct, and notably very insecure, versions of implementations of the cryptographic hash function SHA-1. The GPT models Llama-2-70b-chat-hf, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.1, and zephyr-7b-alpha are used. The GPT models are prompted to re-write each function using a modified version of the localGPT framework to provide word embedding context of the full source code and header files to the model, resulting in over 150, 000 function re-write GPT output text blocks, approximately 50, 000 of which were able to be parsed as C code and subsequently compiled. The generated code is analyzed for being compilable, correctness of the algorithm, memory leaks, compiler optimization stability, and character distance to the reference implementation. Remarkably, several generated function variants have a high implementation security risk of being correct for some test vectors, but incorrect for other test vectors. Additionally, many function implementations were not correct to the reference algorithm of SHA-1, but produced hashes that have some of the basic characteristics of hash functions. Many of the function re-writes contained serious flaws such as memory leaks, integer overflows, out of bounds accesses, use of uninitialized values, and compiler optimization instability. Compiler optimization settings and SHA-256 hash checksums of the compiled binaries are used to cluster implementations that are equivalent but may not have identical syntax—using this clustering, over 100, 000 distinct and correct (up to input-output validation checking) versions of the SHA-1 codebase were generated, by permuting between versions of the four component functions, where each component C function of the reference implementation is different from the original code.
authors: Elijah Pelofske; Vincent E. Urias; Lorie M. Liebrock

title: Reinforcement Learning for Software Vulnerability Analysis: A Systematic Review with Emphasis on C/C++ Source Code and Static Analysis
authors: Bruno Caro-Vásquez; Carola Figueroa-Flores; Gastón Márquez

title: Climate Risk Intelligence Index (CRII): An AI-Augmented Satellite-Based Climate Vulnerability Assessment Framework for India
abstract: Climate change has emerged as a major global challenge affecting environmental sustainability, hydrological stability, urban resilience, and ecosystem health. Conventional climate vulnerability assessment systems primarily rely on static rule-based frameworks and isolated environmental indicators, limiting contextual interpretability and adaptive reasoning across geographically diverse regions. This paper proposes the Climate Risk Intelligence Index (CRII), an AI augmented satellite-based climate vulnerability assessment framework for large-scale climate intelligence generation across India. The proposed system integrates multi-source Earth observation datasets including MODIS Land Surface Temperature (LST), MODIS NDVI vegetation indices, GHSL urban built-up datasets, ERA5 rainfall reanalysis data, and satellite derived hydrological flood exposure indicators from the JRC Global Surface Water dataset to compute a composite climate vulnerability index. India was spatially partitioned into approximately 3,840 geospatial grid cells for localized environmental risk analysis using grid-wise zonal statistical extraction. In addition to geospatial climate-risk computation, the framework incorporates a Large Language Model (LLM)-based reasoning layer powered by the Groq API and the llama-3.1-8b-instant model for contextual environmental interpretation, dominant-risk identification, and interactive climate intelligence generation. Experimental analysis demonstrated consistent climate-risk characterization across flood-prone coastal regions, metropolitan urban clusters, ecologically sensitive landscapes, and high-temperature arid zones. The AI reasoning module achieved low-latency inference responses of approximately 1–3 seconds per query while improving interpretability and contextual explanation quality compared to earlier rule-based approaches. The proposed CRII framework demonstrates the potential of integrating remote sensing, geospatial analytics, and explainable AI-driven reasoning for scalable climate vulnerability assessment and environmental decision support systems.
authors: Rajarajeswari Subramanian; Shravya H; Sneha Sneha; Yamini K

title: From LLMs to MLLMs to Agents: A Survey of Emerging Paradigms in Jailbreak Attacks and Defenses within LLM Ecosystem
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly evolving from single-modal systems to multimodal LLMs and intelligent agents, expanding their capabilities while introducing new security risks. This paper presents a systematic survey of the complexity of jailbreak attacks and defense mechanisms within the expanding LLM ecosystem. We first trace the developmental trajectory from LLMs to MLLMs and Agents, highlighting the core security challenges emerging at each stage. Next, we categorize mainstream jailbreak techniques from the attack impact and attacker permissions perspectives, and provide comprehensive analysis of representative attack methods, related datasets, and evaluation metrics. On the defense side, we organize existing strategies based on response timing and technical approach, offering a structured understanding of their implementation. Furthermore, we identify key limitations in existing surveys, such as insufficient attention to agent-specific security issues, absence of a clear taxonomy for hybrid jailbreak methods, lack of detailed analysis of experimental setups, and outdated coverage of recent advancements. To address these limitations, we provide an updated synthesis of recent work and introduce future research directions in areas such as dataset construction, evaluation framework optimization, and strategy generalization. Our study aims to deepen the understanding of jailbreak mechanisms and promote the development of adaptive defenses for LLMs.
authors: Yanxu Mao; Tiehan Cui; Peipei Liu; Datao You; Hongsong Zhu
venue: ACM Transactions on Knowledge Discovery from Data

title: A Review of Source Code Vulnerability Detection Methods Based on Large Language Models: Models, Techniques, and Evaluation
abstract: In source code vulnerability detection, large language models (LLMs) are no longer used only as substitutes for traditional fixed classifiers. With prompt design, parameter fine-tuning, and program-context information, they can judge whether code contains vulnerabilities and can also provide suspicious locations and explanatory evidence. This paper takes lightweight code Transformers and large-scale language models as two main lines of discussion. It reviews methods for input construction, task adaptation, the use of program-analysis information, and multi-model collaboration, and compares them in terms of datasets, evaluation metrics, and deployment conditions. Existing studies show that code pretraining, prompt engineering, supervised fine-tuning, and structural-information enhancement can improve detection or explanation results on specific benchmarks. However, such improvements are easily affected by duplicate samples, label noise, random splits, temporal leakage, and changes in model versions, which may lead to overestimated performance. Therefore, model evaluation should not rely on a single metric alone. It should also report the data source, detection granularity, temporal or project-level isolation, false-positive cost, and whether generated explanations can be verified by program evidence. On this basis, this paper further discusses an application approach centered on data governance, strict data splitting, uncertainty calibration, and SAST-LLM-human collaboration. The discussion is limited to source-code-level vulnerability detection, localization, and classification, and does not cover network intrusion detection, malware analysis, smart-contract-specific detection, vulnerability generation, or automatic repair.
authors: Letong Qin

title: An AHP Framework for Evaluating Large Language Models in Software Vulnerability Assessment
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can assist software security review, but detecting more weaknesses may increase false alarms, unreliable patches, or higher costs. This methodological paper specifies a reproducible Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) framework for evaluating LLM-assisted vulnerability assessment in a synthetic banking-information application. Applying the framework to a local operational banking system was not feasible because obtaining the required security approvals was difficult; no production banking infrastructure was tested. Six objectives are linked to measurable indicators covering ground-truth completeness, detection, classification and severity assessment, secure remediation, reliability and resource use, and decision sensitivity. The protocol specifies 12 vulnerable and 12 corrected variants, four scenarios, repeated runs, blinded adjudication, CVSS v4.0 assessment, regression tests, and paired analysis. A comparison with SecurityEval, CyberSecEval, CyberSecEval 2, and BountyBench positions the proposed contribution as linking verified outcomes to stakeholder priorities rather than demonstrating superior benchmark performance. An exact reciprocal AHP example uses weights of 0.40, 0.30, 0.20, and 0.10. A separate simulation yields group weights of 0.3565, 0.2920, 0.2187, and 0.1328, with a consistency ratio of 0.0008. These are constructed examples, not elicited expert judgments. No LLM benchmarking was performed, and no model ranking is claimed. Empirical validation requires archived runs, independently assessed outcomes, and human stakeholder judgments; production transfer additionally requires institutional authorization and service-specific validation.
authors: Mohamed Abugharsa; Ali M Abdulshahed
venue: Scientific Journal of Faculty of Education Misurata University

title: PGNexus-AI: An Intelligent and Secure Natural-Language PostgreSQL Administration Framework
abstract: Modern teams depend on PostgreSQL for mission-critical workloads, yet administration is still done by hand-writing SQL in disconnected tools such as psql, pgAdmin and DBeaver, while AI assistants such as GitHub Copilot have no live connection to the database and cannot read its schema, execution plans or error output. LLM-generated SQL also introduces new injection-style security risks. This paper presents PGNexus-AI, a PostgreSQL-only desktop IDE that combines Google Gemini, Gemma 4 and GitHub Copilot behind a schema-grounded orchestration layer. It provides natural-language-to-SQL generation, execution-plan-driven query optimization, automatic error diagnosis and correction, and AI-generated schema documentation with column-relationship mapping. A defense-in-depth safety layer (parameterization, query preview and confirmation, read-only and sandbox execution, role-based scoping and injection screening) protects production databases, and GitHub integration version-controls SQL and migrations. We describe the architecture, methodology and an evaluation plan covering efficiency, reliability, optimization and security.
authors: Shruti Mahendra Raskar; Dr. Brijendra Gupta

title: Autonomous hardware security evaluation from reconnaissance to physical validation
abstract: Abstract Physical hardware-security evaluation requires both target-specific reasoning and control of laboratory instruments. This study presents a large language model (LLM) agent that links reconnaissance, vulnerability hypotheses, laser fault-injection experiments and reporting through human approval gates. The agent reverse-engineers firmware and instruction behaviour, combines this evidence with documentation and chip imagery, and generates bounded experiments with predefined rules for classifying outcomes. On an ATmega328P microcontroller, agent-derived experiments produced a skipped processor load instruction, acceptance of an incorrect personal identification number (PIN), and the same two-byte Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) encrypted-output difference in 14 trials, with 29 paired fault-free controls. Photon-emission imaging narrowed the physical search region. A second campaign on an Artix-7 field-programmable gate array (FPGA) tested transfer to programmable logic using firmware-binary analysis, optical-to-layout registration and cryptographic-output classification. Recorded agent and operator decisions connect observations to experimental revisions and documented conclusions, demonstrating an autonomous workflow across two hardware architectures.
authors: Raphael Viera

title: Measuring Users' Security and Privacy Concerns About Third-Party Community Bots on Discord
abstract: Third-party community-based bots are central to how social platforms such as Discord work. They moderate content, manage roles, play music, and support AI-assisted conversations across millions of servers. Yet when a bot is installed in a server, it can access messages, user profiles, and server metadata concerning members who did not participate in the installation decision, with no standardized way to communicate the associated security and privacy implications. In this paper, we analyze 23,102 third-party Discord bots and 183,142 user reviews spanning 49 detected languages and five years of feedback (2021-2026). We employ LLM-based knowledge distillation and fine-tune a DeBERTa-based classifier to identify candidate security and privacy (S&P)-relevant reviews. After manually validating the complete classifier-positive set, we retain 8,832 reviews identified as S&P-relevant, representing an observed pipeline yield of 4.82%, and map them to a 31-theme S&P taxonomy extending prior work. Our results show that S&P-related reviews focus heavily on Data Sharing (30.5%) and Data Collection (16.2%). Confession and anonymity bots have pipeline-identified SPRRs above 50%, more than ten times the ecosystem-wide pipeline yield of 4.82%. Star ratings may obscure the frequency and valence of S&P-related discussion, while conventional metadata features, such as permission count and administrator status, show only weak associations with user-reported S&P concerns. We then build BotLens, a proof-of-concept auditing framework that combines review-derived S&P signals with bot metadata to provide on-demand decision support for the community-based bot ecosystem. BotLens exposes six tools through a Model Context Protocol server, supporting bot-level checkups, server-wide comparison, and integration with AI agents.
authors: Kofi Ampomah; Tu Le

title: Enhancing LLM-Based Vulnerability Detection via Representation-Aware Logical Ensemble
abstract: Automated vulnerability detection in C source code is a long-standing challenge, as traditional static analysis tools often trade precision for scalability and struggle with complex vulnerability patterns. Recently, large language models (LLMs) have shown promising results; yet, most approaches rely on a single code representation, implicitly assuming uniform suitability across vulnerability types. In this work, we systematically study LLM-based vulnerability detection under multiple code representations, including raw source code, Abstract Syntax Trees (AST), and Control Flow Graphs (CFG). Through extensive empirical analysis, we show that different representations exhibit complementary strengths, with specific views being more effective for particular classes of vulnerabilities. Building on these findings, we propose a Representation-Aware Logical Ensemble (RALE) that integrates LLMs trained on different code representations through explicit logical rules and majority voting. While single-representation models achieve up to 73% F1-score, our integrated approach reaches 78% F1-score, with commensurate gains in accuracy, precision, and recall, consistently outperforming individual models. These results highlight the importance of explicitly leveraging complementary code representations when combining LLMs for effective vulnerability detection.
authors: Francesco C. Grasso; Pietro Liguori; R. Natella; D. Cotroneo

title: NameTrap: Steering AI Coding Agents Toward Security Vulnerabilities via Variable Names
abstract: AI coding agents routinely clone repositories, install packages, and read source code obtained from the Web, so publicly hosted code becomes part of the context that shapes the code they write. We show that this Web-borne context can be weaponized without any explicit instruction. We present NameTrap, a source-code poisoning attack that only renames identifiers in third-party Python files to steer AI coding agents toward attacker-targeted Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) vulnerabilities. An attacker-side coding agent iteratively aligns identifiers with a CWE-specific naming convention and confirms through local probe completions that the renamed file elicits the target weakness, while the released bait contains neither instructions nor vulnerable statements. We evaluate NameTrap across six AI coding agents, ten underlying language models, and four vulnerability categories: CWE-78, CWE-79, CWE-327, and CWE-502. Starting from files whose clean versions never yield the targeted CWE, identifier-level manipulation achieves overall attack success rates of 22.5\% to 56.0\% across the six agents, reaching 75.0\% for certain agent--model configurations, and substantially outperforms random renaming, neutral renaming, and the prior identifier-poisoning attack XOXO. The attack remains effective under Traditional Chinese prompts and transfers across models, while a security-reminder defense fails to consistently prevent vulnerability introduction. Moreover, three AI-based security analyzers and four static analyzers report none of the targeted weaknesses in the poisoned files. These findings expose an overlooked attack surface of agents that consume Web content: seemingly harmless variable names in untrusted, Web-hosted code can compromise the security of downstream software.
authors: Chieh‐Yuan Chang; Guan‐Wei Chen; Chia-Yi Hsu; Chih Yang; Chia-Mu Yu; Chun-Ying Huang

title: Directed Symbolic Execution for Path Feasibility Analysis]{Directed Symbolic Execution for Path Feasibility Analysis in Software Security Testing
abstract: Abstract Symbolic execution can assess the feasibility of interprocedural control flow paths, including those associated with reports from static security analyzers, helping reduce unnecessary investigation of false-positive reports. However, its computational cost limits its practical application. This study aims to develop and implement a method for interprocedural path feasibility analysis using directed symbolic execution, assess its scalability across paths of varying length and complexity, and evaluate its effectiveness as a post-processing step for static analyzers. The proposed method is based on symbolic execution. Because symbolic execution is resource-demanding, the method directs execution by eliminating redundant program branches unrelated to the path being verified. To enable automated path feasibility analysis, the study presents automatic symbolization approaches supporting variables and memory locations with unknown values, entry-point function parameters, dynamically linked functions return values and pointer arguments. To mitigate path explosion in loops, the method limits loop iteration counts without terminating symbolic execution. The method achieved 95.3% recall on the extracted GNU Coreutils paths. Integration with MLH static analysis tool increased precision from 56.6% to 100% on the evaluated Juliet subset while preserving recall. When applied to Infer and Clang Static Analyzer reports, the method maintained or improved their baseline performance, whereas KLEEF reduced the corresponding F1-scores to 0 and 0.074, respectively. The results indicate that the proposed method scales effectively for real-world programs, improving static analysis precision while preserving detected true positives on the benchmarks.
authors: Hovhannes Movsisyan; Hripsime Hovhannisyan; Tigran Avagyan; Hayk Aslanyan

title: When Static Reachability Says No: Checking Joern-Based Negative Verdicts for Python Against Execution
abstract: A negative reachability verdict removes a finding from human review. We check such verdicts against execution. Our pipeline, SourceLens, maps Semgrep findings to a Python program's call graph, whose edges a query takes from the calls that Joern links in its code property graph. We ran two command-line programs from the PyCG macro-benchmark, in which the benchmark's manual call graph and Joern disagree, under coverage and recorded the calls between their functions. On these edges, 123 functions of asciinema are unreachable from the program's entry points. The project's own integration script executes 86 of them, and all our runs 113. In Sublist3r, 19 of 24 are executed. The latest Joern release gives the same verdicts. The missing calls go through values, such as classes and functions passed around, or have no call expression, as in with blocks and property reads. In asciinema, four missing edges make 50 of the 113 executed functions reachable. The manual call graphs also lack observed calls, in asciinema many of them property reads and with blocks, which the benchmark may not count as calls. A rule that turns negative verdicts into unknown recovers 62 of the 113 and 15 of the 19, mostly through dunder and private method names. It recovers 0 of the 5 security findings with a negative verdict, all in executed functions. Its selectivity cannot be measured, as only 10 and 5 negative verdicts were not executed, and under library entry-point models it degrades every negative verdict.
authors: Artur Zięba-Kozarzewski; Bartosz Grzegorzewski

title: ReX-GG: a LLM Ensemble Pipeline for Relation-extraction and Graph Generation
abstract: Current LLM ensemble frameworks focus on multi-step setups with additional modules for answer ranking, often opting for token and span analysis rather than structured outputs, leading to heavyweight architectures with potential fail states along the pipeline. Faster, lighter solutions are more vulnerable to hallucination propagation and can lack output control in more complex pipelines. This paper proposes a customisable, lightweight ensemble workflow of coordinated Large Language Models that leverages JSON-structured outputs and anonymous peer-review ranking to mitigate hallucinatory outputs and single-model failure points. The pipeline is demonstrated on a relation extraction task applied to popular science articles in English, targeting four ontologically-grounded relation types (strong causation, weak causation, contrastive, and compositional), with semantic node canonicalisation and interactive, colour-coded HTML causal graphs as the final output. Performance is evaluated through an anonymous user study, achieving an average perceived accuracy of 0.778 against a human-annotated gold standard. The modular architecture supports flexible deployment across both API-based and in-house LLM setups, and the full framework is released under an open license to foster reproducibility and collaborative research.
authors: Giacomo Magnifico; Eduard Barbu

title: Prompt Less, Infer More: Static Analysis-Guided LLM Type Annotation for Python
abstract: Type annotations improve the maintainability and reliability of Python programs, but many real-world projects remain under-annotated because manual annotation is time-consuming and error-prone. Recent neural and LLM-based type inference systems can recover missing annotations, yet they often trade accuracy for efficiency. Existing approaches often fail to exploit project-wide type evidence, or do so inefficiently through unnecessary model calls and noisy prompts. We present SALT, an LLM-based type inference system guided by static analysis. SALT integrates static analysis with LLM inference to resolve types statically, prioritize LLM queries, and construct concise type-aware context. To demonstrate the effectiveness of SALT, we evaluated it on 12 real-world Python projects. SALT achieves the best accuracy among the evaluated systems and reduces estimated LLM cost by up to 78.5% compared with a strong coding-assistant baseline. It also shows similar cost savings with the frontier model GPT-5.5, demonstrating that SALT remains effective with strong LLMs.
authors: Wonseok Oh; Michael Pradel; Hakjoo Oh

title: When LLM Architectures Meet Smart Contract Vulnerability Detection: a Replication Study
abstract: Smart contracts are immutable programs deployed on blockchain platforms, where vulnerabilities can translate directly into financial loss. Among the techniques proposed for their detection, recent work has relied increasingly on Large Language Models (LLMs) guided by carefully crafted prompts. However, the evidence accumulated so far rests almost entirely on the dense Transformer architecture behind the GPT line and on model snapshots already scheduled for deprecation, leaving open the question of whether the reported behaviors reflect a general property of LLMs or an artifact of that specific design. This paper presents an extended replication of the empirical study by Chen et al. on LLM-based smart contract vulnerability detection. We replicate the original protocol on GPT-4 as a baseline, followed by a differentiated replication, executing the protocol on representative models based on Mixture-of-Experts and RNN-like designs, together with an attempted preliminary evaluation of State Space Models. The exact replication confirms the findings of Chen et al., including the high-recall, low-precision detection pattern they report on GPT-4. Nevertheless, the differentiated replication shows that this pattern does not transfer uniformly across the evaluated models. Those from the same architectural family may also exhibit different behaviors, indicating that architectural family alone is insufficient to predict the resulting detection profile. We observe the same qualitative dense-Transformer profile in both GPT-4 and Gemma-3, despite a gap of roughly two orders of magnitude in parameter counts, whereas two Mixture-of-Experts models from different lineages exhibit qualitatively divergent behaviors, indicating that architectural family alone is insufficient to predict the detection profile.
authors: Gerardo Iuliano; Gabriele De Vito; Dario Di Nucci

title: RoleFUZZER: User-Behaviour Fuzzing for Role-Specification Adherence in Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often conditioned into specific roles such as tutors, interviewers, or agents acting for an organisation, through system prompts that specify how they should behave. The extent to which they can actually adhere to these role specifications under multi-turn interactions with realistic and potentially problematic users is understudied. To address this, we propose user behaviour fuzzing, a guided search over plausible user behaviours that can lead a model to violate its role specification, and introduce RoleFUZZER, a framework that adapts coverage-guided fuzzing from software testing to operationalise the search. RoleFUZZER constructs scenarios guided by a user-behaviour coverage grid that crosses a grounded taxonomy of user interaction types and the role specification of the model under test i.e. what is under pressure. With RoleFUZZER, we evaluate LLMs across five role specifications, including tutor, financial advisor, AI interviewer, antagonistic roleplay character, and web agent under organisational policies. Across simulated and validated conversations in 15 campaigns, the framework reaches >= 89% coverage of the 64-cell behaviour grid for every model and role tested, and surfaces specification-grounded failure patterns. At an equal budget of conversations, removing the RoleFUZZER grid and asking an LLM to generate specification targeting users free-form lowers coverage to 39-69% with fewer kinds of violations. The same specification can also fail in opposite directions. For e.g., on the antagonist, open-weight target models override the player's safety signals, while Claude Haiku 4.5 breaks character instead. RoleFUZZER offers a tractable way to uncover vulnerabilities in LLMs across role specifications by testing diverse user behaviours that are likely to violate them.
authors: Kshitish Ghate; Michael Saxon; Tadayoshi Kohno; Aylin Caliskan

title: Auditable Belief Updates as a Missing Safety Layer for LLM-Powered Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being used as cognitive interfaces that shape how users interpret evidence, communicate, and make decisions. As deployed systems become more multimodal, tool-using, and multi-agent, safety failures no longer arise only from isolated harmful outputs, but also from how agents update, store, and propagate epistemic commitments across retrieval, memory, tools, and peer communication. In this paper, we define belief as an engineering abstraction for evidence-based commitments that guide downstream action. Building on this view, we propose the Explicit Belief Multi-Agent System (EB-MAS), which externalizes belief states into a structured substrate, uses belief operators to propose candidate updates, and applies a Cognitive Firewall to bound or reject updates that are weakly evidenced but strongly driven by vulnerability cues. We also discuss the risk of group belief at the group level, including manufactured consensus, collusion, and cascading misinformation, and outline practical integration challenges around grounding, false positives, scalability, and ethical misuse. Therefore, scalable agent safety requires not only better output filtering or stronger base models, but also explicit interfaces for tracing, calibrating, and constraining belief revision at runtime.
authors: Zhuoyun Li; Boxuan Wang; Jinwei Hu; Xiaowei Huang; Yi Dong

title: Is it my preference? Role Grounding Attack against Agent's Memory via Social Interaction
abstract: LLM-based agents now share experiences on social platforms and remember new preferences to enhance their performance. However, existing memory systems contain a vulnerability in role-to-principal attribution that attackers can exploit. We identify Role Grounding Misattribution, in which an attacker-designed interaction causes the victim agent to incorrectly record a preference from the attacker as a preference of the victim's user. Specifically, we are the first to formalize Role Grounding Attack (RGA), an attack model that exploits this vulnerability through nested conversation structures. In the memory formation stage, an experience-sharing post quoting a conversation between the attacker agent and its user is published, which explicitly identifies its publisher. The inner conversation expresses preferences from the user of the attacker agent. When the victim agent remembers preferences from this nested structure, its memory loses the context binding and grounds the attacker's preference to the victim's user instead. In the memory retrieval stage, the misattributed preference persists and influences the victim agent's decisions when it encounters relevant scenarios. We instantiate RGA as tool selection manipulation and privacy leakage. Tool selection manipulation causes a tool-call preference to be misattributed to the victim's user, steering the victim toward an attacker-controlled tool. Privacy leakage extends this by misattributing both a tool-call preference and a task-requirement preference to the victim's user. The victim selects the attacker's tool, then includes sensitive information in tool arguments to satisfy the task requirement. We evaluate RGA across five mainstream memory systems and six language models. Tool manipulation and privacy leakage both achieve high attack success rates. These results call for stronger role grounding.
authors: Haoran Bu; Yiting Shen; Litian Zhang; Ruihan Hu; Xi Zhang

title: ANGLER: Verifier-Grounded Benchmarking with an Adaptive Attacker for Web Agents
abstract: Web agents are increasingly deployed to complete tasks autonomously on real websites, where adversarially injected content can induce them to perform unauthorized actions. Existing evaluations primarily use fixed attacks or focus on a single attack type, and evaluate attacks at the text level rather than through real state changes, thus underestimating how vulnerable agents are to diverse attacks. To address the gap, we introduce REEF, a benchmark of red-teaming executable environments with faithful verification for measuring the security vulnerabilities of web agents. REEF covers 9 verifier-grounded websites spanning travel, commerce, productivity, media, and communication, and pairs every authentic benign task with a malicious objective delivered through 5 attack types at both the user and the environment level. REEF's state-based verifiers provide the execution feedback that drives ANGLER, an adaptive near-miss-guided lure evolution framework for red-teaming. Rather than evaluating a fixed attack set, ANGLER uses outcomes from prior rollouts to guide LLM-based attack mutation and candidate selection, prioritizing near-miss seeds during refinement. Across 8 VLM-based web agents, ANGLER achieves an end-to-end attack success rate (ASR) of 20.36%, compared with 15.24% for the non-adaptive setting. Compared with attack-free execution on the same benign tasks, attacks generated by ANGLER reduce benign task success rate (BSR) from 61.9% to 44.4%.
authors: Yini Huang; Aiwen LU; Zhen Sun; Yi Han; Yuzhi Zhao; Jiaheng Wei

title: Characterizing Recoverable Expert-Utilization Signatures in Fine-Tuned Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
abstract: As Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models are increasingly deployed in distributed environments, from federated learning to edge-cloud systems, their architecture harbors an underexplored landscape of security vulnerabilities. Moving beyond textual analysis, we uncover structural memorization: a novel vulnerability where a fine-tuned model memorizes not only its training data but also the internal pathway used to process it, creating a characteristic routing fingerprint unique to the training process. We provide comprehensive empirical evidence that structural memorization emerges consistently even from a few samples, and that its intensity is directly influenced by the choice of trainable modules. We show that these memorized expert pathways can be stealthily recovered through the model's unconditional generation, using only routing and output logits, with no knowledge of the fine-tuning data or procedure. In distributed deployments, this vulnerability is amplified as routing information is exposed at multiple trust boundaries, including federated aggregation points, edge-cloud interfaces, and multi-tenant monitoring systems. Recovery exposes a critical blind spot: traditional membership inference metrics, viewed through the lens of expert routing, fail to identify memorized data corresponding to these structural pathways. To close this gap, we devise composite metrics combining reference model tail likelihood with complexity-aware normalization, significantly improving detection of memorized routing structures. This enables adversaries to pinpoint critical experts shaped by fine-tuning, whether dominant or dormant, and execute targeted attacks such as router manipulation or backdoor injection in realistic distributed settings where attackers lack training data but can observe routing patterns across system components.
authors: Fei Wang; Baochun Li; Bo Li

title: InferD: A Honeypot Framework for AI Inference Infrastructure
abstract: Large language model serving stacks, commercial inference APIs, vector databases, and agent orchestration gateways are now ex- posed on the public internet and indexed by commodity scanners within hours of deployment. The threat characteristics of this sur- face are only beginning to be measured, and the honeypot frame- works that could measure it were designed for conventional net- work services rather than for AI infrastructure. In fact, emulating an AI service is a distinct deception problem: the observable behavior of the service, including model inventories, token formats, tool-call protocols, and authorization flows, must be reproduced faithfully, while the underlying computation, model inference and tool ex- ecution, must never occur. We present InferD, a low-interaction honeypot framework organized around a single principle we call deception without inference: every request an adversary can observe is answered from static response pools, and nothing an adversary submits is ever executed. InferD decomposes the emulation into four deception planes, transport, service protocol, vulnerability surface, and agentic session, adds a provenance plane that links a planted credential to evidence of downstream model-mediated processing.
authors: Hicham Hammouchi; Gabriele Lenzini

title: Prevented is Not Protected: What Attack Success Rate Hides about RAG
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is vulnerable to knowledge poisoning, where adversaries manipulate retrieved evidence to influence model outputs. Existing defenses are primarily evaluated using attack success rate (ASR), which obscures defense-induced failures and the mechanisms behind apparent attack prevention. To address this issue, this work introduces \textbf{Aligned RAG Evaluation}, a matched-query protocol that jointly examines clean and poisoned responses, with and without defense. By combining matched conditions analysis, LLM-judge endorsement, and retrieval dependence controls, the proposed framework distinguishes prevented from introduced failures, target mentions from LLM endorsement, and single-passage influence from evidence composition. Experiments on HotpotQA and Natural Questions reveal that existing defenses can introduce unexpected target-positive answers, although they can prevent some attacks, while evaluation criteria can also change defense rankings. Our findings expose critical blind spots in ASR-based evaluation and motivate a more comprehensive assessment of RAG poisoning defenses. The code and the evaluation artifact are available at https://github.com/chxhana/aligned-rag-eval.
authors: Chahana Dahal; Zuobin Xiong

title: Watermark Basins: Black-Box Detection of Distilled LLMs
abstract: Proprietary language models and their reasoning traces are vulnerable to API-based distillation, where an adversary trains a student model on the teacher model's outputs. To obtain evidence of distillation, model providers can watermark the teacher's outputs, aiming to leave a radioactive signal in the student's outputs. Existing black-box detectors search for such radioactivity using token-level statistics of the suspect model's outputs. However, token-level signals are not always detectable, for instance when the distillation traces are sampled at a low temperature. In this work, we discover the watermark basin, a persistent signal that enables more reliable watermark detection: during fine-tuning, watermarked teacher traces embed a distinct, key-specific geometric signal in parameter space that lies orthogonal to the ordinary task-specific fine-tuning subspace. Building on this, we introduce Watermark Basin Alignment (WM-Basin), a black-box watermark detector that queries the suspect model through its API, without access to its weights or logits. WM-Basin maps generated text to gradient representations using a fixed clean probe model, projects out the ordinary fine-tuning task directions, and tests whether the residual gradient aligns with the watermark basin induced by the watermark key. We evaluate WM-Basin extensively across diverse teacher models and student architectures (from 135M to 8.2B parameters) distilled on mathematical reasoning. At a strict 0.1% false-positive rate, WM-Basin detects 79% of distilled models at n-gram=1 and 45% at n-gram=3, substantially improving over the state-of-the-art token-level baseline (29% and 1.3%, respectively). Because the watermark signal resides in a persistent basin, it survives post-distillation modifications including quantization, pruning, and reinforcement-learning post-training.
authors: Hongyan Chang; Hady Elsahar; Tom Sander; Pierre Fernandez; Saeed Mahloujifar; Sylvestre-Alvise Rebuffi; Tomáš Souček; Tuan Tran; Valeriu Lacatusu; Surya Parimi; Rashel Moritz; Vanessa Stark; Alexandre Mourachko

title: CHORD: Cross-Model Hallucination Detection via Relational Graph Discrimination
abstract: Hallucination detection is critical for deploying large language models (LLMs) in real-world applications. Due to strong empirical performance, internal representation-based methods have emerged as the prevailing direction for detecting hallucinations, yet they remain largely model-specific and often fail to generalize to unseen LLMs. In this paper, we study an important yet underexplored problem, termed cross-model hallucination detection (CMHD), which aims to train hallucination detectors on source LLMs while ensuring performance on unseen target LLMs. The core challenge of CMHD lies in cross-model representation heterogeneity: hidden states from different LLMs exhibit severe semantic inconsistency, which limits the transferability of classical representation-based detectors. Through analysis and empirical validation, we show that relational structures over layers, tokens, and features capture transferable detection signals despite semantic inconsistency. Based on this observation, we propose cross-model hallucination detection via heterogeneity-oriented relational discrimination (CHORD), a relational graph discrimination framework that represents hidden states as joint relational graphs over layers, tokens, and features. It feeds these graphs into relation-aware attention to obtain structure-aware features, and uses meta-learning to shape these features toward transferable detection signals. Extensive experiments show that CHORD outperforms representative detection methods in cross-model generalization. Code is available at https://github.com/MiracleworkerD/CHORD.
authors: Yongxin Deng; Zhen Fang; Guansong Pang; Sharon Li; Ling Chen

title: Session-Bound Behavioral Watermarking for Autonomous LLM Agents
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly acting through Web interfaces and external tools. They produce trajectories. Those trajectories may pass through several intermediaries. They can store, modify, or dispute those trajectories. In Web-based agent deployments, trajectories may pass through APIs, marketplaces, and tool servers. As such, a copied or disputed log may not by itself reveal which agent owner produced it. Behavioral watermarking can embed ownership evidence in agent action choices. However, existing methods mainly address detection, removal, rewriting, or imitation. They do not directly test whether repeated observation of watermarked trajectories enables cross-session forgery by exploiting learned action preferences. We formulate this learned-forgery threat and propose AgentAnchor, a session-keyed behavioral watermark for owner attribution from trajectory logs. We derive each step key from a secret key, a fresh public session identifier, and semantic states of recent observations, while a guarded digest of the action-policy state diversifies linear coding rows. It embeds parity evidence through a KL-bounded exponential tilt, and a trusted verifier checks a disputed log without rerunning the agent, using wrong-key calibration and abstention.
authors: Md Facklasur Rahaman; Yong Xiang; Md Palash Uddin; Shang Gao; Guang Hua; Leo Yu Zhang

title: From Ripple to Boundary: Deterministic Impact Boundaries for LLM-Based Software Evolution
abstract: The landscape of software evolution is undergoing a fundamental paradigm shift in the era of Large Language Models. As industrial software engineering increasingly transitions toward design-driven code generation, the bottleneck of evolution has shifted from writing code to maintaining deterministic consistency between multi-source design assets and the generated code. When a design asset changes, LLM agents currently lack a deterministic impact boundary to identify which code must be evolved, leading to two failure modes: hallucinating missing changes or breaking unrelated code. Probabilistic approaches, such as semantic retrieval or text-based diffing, fail to capture the structural ripple effects across highly interconnected design dependencies. We propose a paradigm shift from probabilistic semantic retrieval to deterministic structural constraints. We formalize the design assets as a Knowledge Graph and organize them into a content-addressed Merkle Directed Acyclic Graph. Our key insight reveals a topological isomorphism between the logical ripple effect of a design change and the content hash propagation within the DAG. By leveraging this, we transform ambiguous impact analysis into verifiable structural operations. Through a two-phase diffing process, we extract a precise causal chain that defines the exact modification boundary. This boundary enables deterministic context injection, providing the LLM agent with strictly scoped code and design updates, thereby fundamentally guaranteeing evolution safety. As a by-product, the KG serves as an agent-queryable knowledge base for natural language design retrieval. Early deployment on a large-scale industrial payment platform demonstrates that our mechanism successfully computes the exact impact boundary and generates incremental code modifications that meet the expected design changes.
authors: Jiameng Bai; Zhitao Wang; Long Wang; Keyue Qian; Sai Wu

title: Do Language Models Know What Compelling Scientific Evidence Looks Like?
abstract: Expert scientists excel at weighing empirical findings from multiple sources that vary in both statistical reliability and epistemic relevance. To what extent are language models, which are increasingly driving autonomous discovery systems, capable of such evidence deliberation? We introduce EDB-Bio, a scientific reasoning benchmark curated from real-world data in three biological domains: drug-perturbation transcriptomics, CRISPR screens, and human genome-wide association studies (GWAS). Each of EDB-Bio's 96k episodes presents a sequence of experimental results from published studies and asks the model to predict the probability that a target hypothesis is true. Out-of-the-box, open-weight and frontier models alike demonstrate systematic underconfidence and attain Brier scores comparable to a trivial base-rate forecaster. Post-training against strictly proper scoring rules significantly improves both calibration and discrimination. This calibration pays off downstream: in a sequential experiment selection task, our Ibis0 model is 2.5 times more efficient than the best frontier model. Throughout, quantifying evidence weights as Bayes factors reveals how models update their beliefs over time, whether they agree with expert biologists on relevance, and where they exhibit inconsistencies and biases. Our work extends calibration training and uncertainty analysis to a realistic scientific forecasting setting with applications to human cancer biology. We release all code, data, and trained models.
authors: Conor Igoe; Gabriel Grand; Zane Koch; Albert Bou; Eli Moss; Michaela M. Hinks; Samuel G. Rodriques; Andrew White; Siddharth Narayanan

title: Ontology-guided multi-agent reasoning for explainable differential diagnosis
abstract: Effective differential diagnosis depends on well structured and unambiguous patient case descriptions, since incomplete or ambiguous clinical information readily leads to diagnostic errors and inconsistent reasoning. Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently shown promising capabilities in medical question answering and clinical reasoning; however, even when achieving competitive performance on medical benchmarks, they often rely on pattern recognition learned from training data rather than grounded clinical evidence, and can generate plausible yet unsupported diagnostic conclusions. Their reasoning remains largely opaque, making it difficult for clinicians to assess the evidence and rationale behind a given recommendation. To address this gap, we propose an ontology-guided, multiagent differential diagnosis framework that replicates the iterative reasoning process of physicians. The framework grounds diagnostic inference in a structured, expert-curated medical knowledge base, enabling interpretation of symptoms, clinical findings, or disease relationships, while decomposing diagnosis into explicit, auditable reasoning steps. This ontology-based grounding constrains inference to evidence-backed associations, reducing hallucination and improving diagnostic transparency, traceability, and consistency. The system then identifies the most discriminative missing symptoms and generates targeted follow-up questions to reduce uncertainty through a process that mirrors to clinical inquiry. Together, these components improve the reliability, explainability, and diagnostic accuracy of AI-assisted differential diagnosis. The source code is publicly available.
authors: Roxana Ramona Szomiu; George Ursu; Adrian Groza

title: Distilling the Shape of Uncertainty: What On-Policy Distillation Learns and How to Predict It
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is increasingly adopted in the post-training of large language models. However, a stronger teacher may fail to improve the student. Prior work attributes this to a lack of new knowledge, but what that knowledge is remains unclear. We show that OPD learns not only \textit{how to branch}, i.e., which candidate tokens to consider, but also \textit{where to branch}, i.e., where to keep reasoning paths open. The existing token-overlap metric captures only the former.
